```{=html}
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/cytoscape@3.30.2/dist/cytoscape.min.js"></script>
```

A knowledge graph is three things at once: **entities** with identity, **typed
relationships** between them, and a **shared vocabulary** that gives both a
meaning a machine can act on. Drop any one and you have something else — a
table, a diagram, or a folder of files.

This project has all three. `wdn:J141` is an entity with a stable IRI.
`wdn:deployedAt` is a typed relationship, not a foreign key that happens to
line up. And `wdn:DeadEnd` means something: it is a subclass of `wdn:Node`,
disjoint from `wdn:Link`, and a reasoner can act on that without being told
again.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from rdflib import Graph, RDF, URIRef, Literal
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
import json

g = Graph(); g.parse("data/graph.ttl", format="turtle")
NS = "https://w3id.org/iitb/wdn#"
PFX = [(NS,"wdn:"), ("http://www.w3.org/ns/sosa/","sosa:"),
       ("http://www.w3.org/ns/ssn/","ssn:"),
       ("http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#","rdfs:"),
       ("http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#","owl:"),
       ("http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#","rdf:"),
       ("http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#","geo:"),
       ("http://qudt.org/vocab/unit/","unit:"),
       ("http://purl.org/dc/terms/","dcterms:"),
       ("http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#","xsd:")]
def sh(t):
    t = str(t)
    for p, a in PFX:
        if t.startswith(p): return t.replace(p, a)
    return t

TBOX = {"owl:Class","owl:ObjectProperty","owl:DatatypeProperty","owl:Ontology",
        "owl:FunctionalProperty","owl:Restriction","owl:SymmetricProperty",
        "owl:TransitiveProperty","rdfs:Class","owl:NamedIndividual"}

alltypes = defaultdict(set)
for s_, _, o in g.triples((None, RDF.type, None)):
    ot = sh(o)
    if ot not in TBOX: alltypes[s_].add(ot)
freq = Counter(t for ts in alltypes.values() for t in ts)
# the most specific asserted type is the rarest one
ntype = {s_: min(ts, key=lambda t: freq[t]) for s_, ts in alltypes.items() if ts}

n_entities = len(ntype)
n_rel  = sum(1 for s_, p, o in g if isinstance(o, URIRef) and sh(p) != "rdf:type")
n_attr = sum(1 for s_, p, o in g if isinstance(o, Literal))
n_pred = len({sh(p) for _, p, _ in g})

cells = [(f"{len(g):,}", "triples"), (f"{n_entities:,}", "entities"),
         (f"{n_rel:,}", "relationships"), (f"{n_attr:,}", "attributes"),
         (f"{n_pred}", "distinct predicates"),
         (f"{len(set(ntype.values()))}", "classes in use")]
print('<div class="statbar">')
for n, l in cells:
    print(f'<div><div class="n">{n}</div><div class="l">{l}</div></div>')
print('</div>')
```

## The schema, derived from the data

Most ontology diagrams show what the author *declared*. This one shows what is
actually **asserted in the instance data**: every distinct
(class → predicate → class) pattern, sized by how often it occurs. If a
declared property is never used, it does not appear here.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
schema = Counter()
for s_, p, o in g:
    ps = sh(p)
    if ps == "rdf:type": continue
    a = ntype.get(s_); b = ntype.get(o) if isinstance(o, URIRef) else None
    if a and b: schema[(a, ps, b)] += 1

LAYER = {
 "wdn:Pipe":"network", "wdn:Junction":"network", "wdn:DeadEnd":"network",
 "wdn:Bend":"network", "wdn:WaterDistributionNetwork":"network",
 "wdn:DistrictMeteredArea":"network", "wdn:PipeMaterial":"network",
 "wdn:MonitoringStation":"sensing", "sosa:ObservableProperty":"sensing",
 "wdn:SensorModel":"sensing",
 "wdn:PlacementRationale":"placement", "wdn:TopologyCriterion":"placement",
 "wdn:TerrainCriterion":"placement", "wdn:PressureCriterion":"placement",
 "wdn:DemandCriterion":"placement",
}
def layer(c):
    if c in LAYER: return LAYER[c]
    if "Sensor" in c: return "sensing"
    if "Risk" in c or "Criterion" in c: return "placement"
    return "network"

counts = Counter(ntype.values())
nodes = sorted({a for a,_,_ in schema} | {b for _,_,b in schema})
els = [{"data":{"id":c,"label":c,"n":counts.get(c,0)},"classes":layer(c)} for c in nodes]
for i,((a,p,b),n) in enumerate(schema.items()):
    els.append({"data":{"id":f"e{i}","source":a,"target":b,"label":p,"n":n}})
print('<div id="schema-graph" style="height:560px;border:1px solid #e4e7ea;'
      'border-radius:8px;background:#fbfbfc;"></div>')
print('<p class="muted" style="font-size:12px;margin-top:6px;">'
      'Node size follows instance count; edge thickness follows how often the '
      'pattern occurs. Blue = network, green = sensing, orange = placement. '
      'Drag to rearrange.</p>')
print(f'<script>window.SCHEMA={json.dumps(els)};</script>')
```

```{=html}
<script>

    if(!window.cytoscape||!window.SCHEMA) return setTimeout(draw,120);
    cytoscape({

        {selector:"node", style:{

    });
  }

})();
</script>
```

## What is in it

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
rows = [(c, n, layer(c)) for c, n in counts.most_common() if n > 1]
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["Class", "Instances", "Layer"]).style.hide(axis="index")
```

The three layers are the point. A network model alone cannot say why a node is
instrumented. A sensor inventory alone cannot say what the node it sits on is
connected to. Holding them in one graph means the join already exists.

## Why a graph and not three tables

Take a real question: *which sensors sit on dead ends in the district with the
highest mean elevation?*

Relationally that is a four-way join across a sensor table, a station table, a
node table and a district table, and you must know in advance that those keys
line up. If you later add valves, or a second criterion, the schema changes and
every query that touched it breaks.

In the graph it is a path.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
q = """
PREFIX wdn: <https://w3id.org/iitb/wdn#>
SELECT ?station ?sensor ?node ?dma WHERE {
  ?station wdn:deployedAt ?node .
  ?node a wdn:DeadEnd ; wdn:inDMA ?dma .
  ?station <http://www.w3.org/ns/sosa/hosts> ?sensor .
  ?sensor a wdn:PHSensor .
} LIMIT 1
"""
r = list(g.query(q))
if r:
    st, se, nd, dma = [sh(x) for x in r[0]]
    hops = [(se, "rdf:type", "wdn:PHSensor"), (st, "sosa:hosts", se),
            (st, "wdn:deployedAt", nd), (nd, "rdf:type", "wdn:DeadEnd"),
            (nd, "wdn:inDMA", dma)]
    print('<table class="res" style="font-size:12px;max-width:640px;">')
    print("<thead><tr><th>subject</th><th>predicate</th><th>object</th></tr></thead><tbody>")
    for a, p, b in hops:
        print(f"<tr><td>{a}</td><td><em>{p}</em></td><td>{b}</td></tr>")
    print("</tbody></table>")
```

Five hops, no join keys, and nothing in the query had to know how the data was
stored. Adding valves later adds nodes and edges; it does not invalidate the
question.

## The vocabulary is borrowed, not invented

Reusing established vocabularies is what makes a graph interoperable rather
than a private data structure with extra steps.

| Borrowed from | Used for |
|---|---|
| [SOSA/SSN](https://www.w3.org/TR/vocab-ssn/) | sensors, platforms, observable properties, the hosting relation |
| [QUDT](https://qudt.org) | units and quantity kinds |
| [GeoSPARQL](https://opengeospatial.github.io/ogc-geosparql/) | node geometry as WKT |
| [SKOS](https://www.w3.org/TR/skos-reference/) | definitions, alternate labels, scope notes |

Only what is genuinely specific to water distribution — pipes, dead ends,
district metered areas, placement criteria — is defined here.
